newsitem.title: USA: Novartis unit wins stay on generic Zantac.
newsitem.headline: Novartis unit wins stay on generic Zantac.

text.p: Geneva Pharmaceuticals Inc said Thursday it won a stay order from the U.S. Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals blocking the U.S. unit of Novopharm Ltd from selling ranitidine hydrochloride, the generic version of the ulcer drug Zantac.
Novopharm, the privately-held parent of Novopharm Biotech Inc would have started selling the generic drug beginning today under a licensing arrangement with Glaxo Wellcome, the patent holder.
Geneva, one of the largest pharmaceutical manufacturers in the U.S., is a unit of giant Novartis AG.
Geneva said the Richmond, Va.,-based appellate court will hear the case and render a decision on the marketing exclusivity issue shorter after it reconvenes on September 29.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration could now decide to allow all eligible companies, including Geneva, to make and sell a generic version of the popular drug when its patent expires on July 25.
Stephanie Brooks, a spokeswoman for Novopharm, said her company has filed a petition with the appellate court for a reconsideration of the stay order on an emergency basis.
"We want the court to review the facts and lift the stay order immediately," she said. In the meantime, she said, Novopharm would obey the order.

Geneva, in a statement, said it filed its appeal with the Virginia court to protest a ruling by a federal court in North Carolina last week that no generic pharmaceutical company -- those that make a generic version of a drug after its patent expires -- was entitled to an exclusive marketing window. The rule paved the way for companies to make and sell ranitidine after July 25.
The North Carolina court's ruling overturned a June 18 decision by the FDA to grant GenPharm Inc, a Canadian-based subsidiary of Germany's Merck KGaA, exclusivity through August 29.

Geneva said the FDA decision arose from a citizen petition it filed before the regulatory agency in which it asserted a right to an exclusive marketing widow in ranitidine under statutues designed to encourage the developmenet of generic alternatives.
Geneva said it filed the first so-called Abbreviated New Drug Application or ANDA with the FDA for a certification that the generic drug company does not infringe the innovator's product.

However, according to Novopharm, the North Carolina court's ruling stated that neither Geneva nor Genpharm nor any other pharmaceutical company submitted the first ANDA application for a generic version of Zantac that included the certification.
